paragraphs: Predicting a three-dimensional rotation requires a neural network to produce an output that represents a valid rotation. Several representations are commonly used, including Euler angles, axis-angle coordinates, and unit quaternions. This paper revisits another option: using singular value decomposition, or SVD, to project a matrix onto the set of rotation matrices.

The underlying mathematical procedure, called symmetric orthogonalization, already has established uses in computer vision, including alignment and rotation averaging. The authors investigate its role as a rotation-producing component inside neural networks. They combine a theoretical analysis of projection onto the rotation group with quantitative evaluations across applications involving supervised and unsupervised training.

The reported results show that simply replacing existing rotation representations with SVD orthogonalization achieves state-of-the-art performance in many of the applications studied. This makes the choice of output representation a consequential design decision, even without a more elaborate architectural change. The finding supports SVD as a strong practical option, while retaining the abstract's qualification that no single universally effective rotation representation has been established.
neurips-2020-an-analysis-of-svd-for-deep.tldr: SVD-based projection provides a theoretically analyzed rotation representation that achieves state-of-the-art results in many tested neural-network applications.

paragraphs: Backpropagation trains neural networks effectively, but its usual formulation differs from biologically plausible learning in several ways. Weight updates can depend on information unavailable locally, and external control may be needed to switch between prediction and learning. This paper asks whether a model of brain-like learning can reproduce backpropagation exactly while addressing those differences.

The authors propose a framework in which neurons perform simultaneous local computations, yet the resulting neural weight updates are exactly the same as those produced by backpropagation. This is a stronger correspondence than merely approximating the updates. They then modify the construction into an alternative model that also operates autonomously, addressing the need for external switching of dynamics or plasticity rules.

The contribution is a demonstration that exact backpropagation updates can be compatible with the local learning computations of the proposed framework. The autonomous variant extends that argument to another important aspect of biological plausibility. These constructions provide evidence relevant to whether the brain could perform backpropagation; they are not presented as observations establishing that biological brains actually use the proposed mechanism.
neurips-2020-can-the-brain-do-backpropag.tldr: The paper constructs a biologically plausible learning framework with exact backpropagation weight updates and local computations, then develops an autonomous variant.

paragraphs: Video and text describe events at several scales. Individual frames and words carry fine details, clips and sentences organize shorter events, and whole videos and paragraphs provide broader context. COOT is designed to learn representations that account for this hierarchy, including relationships within each medium and between the visual and textual descriptions.

Its architecture combines three components with distinct responsibilities. Attention-aware feature aggregation uses nearby temporal context within a level, such as within a clip. A contextual transformer models connections between lower-level and higher-level meaning, including clip-to-video and sentence-to-paragraph relationships. A cross-modal cycle-consistency loss provides a further training connection between video and text.

Together, these components make the organization of a video and its description part of the representation-learning problem. The method compares favorably with state-of-the-art approaches on several benchmarks while using few parameters. The stated result supports modeling several levels of meaning jointly: useful video-text correspondence can depend both on local details and on how those details fit into the larger sequence.
neurips-2020-coot-cooperative-hierarchic.tldr: COOT connects local and global video-text meaning through a hierarchical transformer, achieving favorable benchmark results with few parameters.

paragraphs: Collaborative on-device learning lets devices train together without exchanging user data, but communicating model weights can be expensive and requires compatible architectures. This paper instead has devices exchange softmax outputs on a shared, public, unlabeled reference dataset. Those predictions provide a common communication format even when the devices use different neural-network structures.

The distributed distillation algorithm lets each device learn from these shared predictions. Their size scales with the number of classes rather than the number of model parameters. The analysis assumes smooth loss functions, which may be non-convex, and proves that the gradients of all devices' distillation-regularized losses converge to zero with probability one. The stated knowledge-sharing conclusion concerns predictions on the reference data, regardless of devices' local connections.

Simulations support the analysis and show substantially reduced communication with overall accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods, even for a naive implementation. The approach therefore addresses two practical barriers together: transmitting large models and excluding devices with different architectures. The public reference dataset is central because it gives otherwise different models a shared basis for exchanging what they have learned.
neurips-2020-distributed-distillation-fo.tldr: Devices exchange predictions on public reference data to support communication-efficient collaborative learning across different model architectures.

paragraphs: A knowledge base can answer queries by applying logical reasoning to its stored information. Real knowledge bases are incomplete and over-specified, however, so strict deduction can miss questions with real-world answers. Query embedding methods address this by representing both entities and queries in a shared space, allowing inference to relax or generalize beyond explicit logical consequences.

The paper identifies a problem with that flexibility: existing query embedding systems can disagree with deductive reasoning even when a query needs neither relaxation nor generalization. The authors demonstrate this behavior experimentally and introduce a new embedding method designed to be more faithful to deduction. The aim is to improve the relationship between learned inference and the answers already supported by the knowledge base.

The new method performs better on complex queries over incomplete knowledge bases. When inserted into a neural question-answering system, it also yields substantial improvements over the state of the art. These findings connect faithfulness to practical performance: preserving more of the underlying logical behavior can help learned representations answer questions where missing information still makes generalization useful.
neurips-2020-faithful-embeddings-for-kno.tldr: A query embedding method that better respects deductive reasoning improves complex knowledge-base queries and neural question answering.

paragraphs: DBSCAN finds clusters using a graph that connects points within a chosen neighborhood distance, then examines connected regions of high-degree points. Constructing the complete neighborhood graph can require quadratic work in the number of data points. SNG-DBSCAN reduces that expense by clustering from a subsampled version of the graph.

The method needs only similarity queries between pairs of points. It avoids complex data structures requiring access to the points' underlying embeddings. Its runtime is proportional to the sampling rate times the square of the dataset size. Under the paper's theoretical assumptions, a sampling rate around log(n)/n is sufficient for statistical cluster recovery guarantees, giving an n log(n) runtime.

Experiments on large datasets show that sampling as little as 0.1% of the neighborhood graph can retain competitive clustering performance. Reported gains reach over 200-fold faster execution and a 250-fold reduction in RAM consumption relative to scikit-learn's DBSCAN implementation. These are reported experimental outcomes, while the stronger cluster-recovery statement depends on the theoretical assumptions. Together, they support subsampling as a simple way to make density-based clustering less expensive.
neurips-2020-faster-dbscan-via-subsample.tldr: SNG-DBSCAN clusters using a sampled neighborhood graph, offering conditional recovery guarantees and large observed savings in runtime and memory.

paragraphs: Neural-network training usually involves choosing a structure as well as learning its parameters. Firefly neural architecture descent brings those decisions together by progressively growing the network during optimization. The framework can increase both width and depth, allowing its structure to evolve as learning proceeds instead of treating architecture as a separate, fixed choice.

The method follows a steepest-descent idea over a neighborhood of possible network functions. That neighborhood includes diverse candidate structures, so an optimization step can change the architecture as well as its numerical parameters. A Taylor approximation makes the local structural search amenable to a greedy selection procedure, providing a practical route through the candidate changes.

The authors apply the framework to architecture search and continual learning, where retaining earlier knowledge matters while learning new tasks. They report promising results in both settings and show that the approach can learn accurate, resource-efficient architectures that avoid catastrophic forgetting. On a challenging continual image-classification task, the resulting networks are smaller and have higher average accuracy than those learned by the state-of-the-art methods considered.
neurips-2020-firefly-neural-architecture.tldr: Firefly descent jointly optimizes network weights and growing architectures, with promising results in architecture search and continual learning.

paragraphs: Low-density parity-check codes support error correction by organizing constraints and variables in a bipartite graph. Their usual belief-propagation decoder repeatedly updates the graph, often using flooding, where all check and variable nodes are updated together. This paper investigates whether learning the order of individual check-node updates can improve decoding for short to moderate code lengths.

The authors replace flooding with a sequential scheduling policy. They model check-node selection as a multi-armed bandit process with dependent arms and use Q-learning to optimize the policy. Because the possible learning states make this demanding, they also introduce graph-based clustering of check nodes. The clustering partitions the state space while minimizing dependencies between clusters.

The reported results show significantly improved decoding performance compared with other approaches in the literature. They also show a dramatic reduction in decoding complexity once the scheduling policy has been learned. That qualification separates the cost of learning a schedule from the cost of using it. The contribution is therefore both a learned decoding strategy and a graph-informed way to make learning that strategy more manageable.
neurips-2020-learning-to-decode-reinforc.tldr: Reinforcement learning improves check-node scheduling for LDPC decoding, increasing decoding performance and reducing complexity after the policy is learned.

paragraphs: Making a self-attention network larger leaves a design choice: add more layers or widen the representations inside them. Earlier findings suggested that width could be as useful as depth, challenging the expectation that additional layers always provide a particularly efficient use of capacity. This paper studies how that tradeoff changes with network width.

The theoretical analysis predicts a width-dependent transition between regimes where depth is efficient and where it is inefficient. Systematic experiments varying networks from 6 to 48 layers reveal the predicted behaviors. The authors use these results to provide quantitative guidance for allocating depth and width at a given overall network size.

The guidance extends to very large self-attention models. Under the paper's analysis, GPT3 is too deep for its size, and a width of 30,000 is identified as optimal for a one-trillion-parameter self-attention network. These are conclusions of the proposed allocation guidelines. The broader implication is that depth and width should be increased together according to their interaction, rather than treating more layers as an independently reliable route to efficient scaling.
neurips-2020-limits-to-depth-efficiencie.tldr: Theory and experiments identify a width-dependent limit to the benefits of depth in self-attention and guide depth-to-width allocation.

paragraphs: Neural populations can represent variables such as head direction or spatial location even when those variables are not directly accessible to an experimenter. This paper introduces an unsupervised probabilistic model that jointly estimates the hidden state and how individual neurons represent it. Its central choice is to allow hidden states to occupy non-Euclidean spaces.

The manifold Gaussian process latent variable model, or mGPLVM, places a shared latent variable on a specified manifold, such as a sphere, torus, or rotation group. Non-parametric tuning curves describe each neuron's response to that shared state. Cross-validation can compare models with different candidate topologies, and variational inference provides a way to quantify uncertainty in the inferred representation.

The authors validate the approach using synthetic datasets and neural recordings from fruit-fly and mouse circuits known to encode head direction. In both biological settings, the model recovers the expected ring topology for a single angular variable. This demonstrates why latent geometry matters: a circular behavioral quantity can be represented using its corresponding structure while the model also learns how neurons participate in encoding it.
neurips-2020-manifold-gplvms-for-discove.tldr: mGPLVM infers hidden neural representations on non-Euclidean manifolds and recovers the expected ring structure in head-direction recordings.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover the inputs and hidden variables of a stochastic multilayer neural network from its observed output. The unknown quantities are matrices, with statistical relationships along both rows and columns. That structure makes the problem relevant to matrix imputation, signal recovery with deep generative priors, mixed and multitask regression, and certain two-layer network-learning problems.

The authors extend Multi-Layer Vector Approximate Message Passing into a matrix-valued algorithm called ML-Mat-VAMP. The theoretical contribution is an exact prediction of its performance in a particular random large-system limit. For unknown matrices of size N by d, N grows without bound while d remains fixed, so the guarantee concerns a specific asymptotic regime.

For the two-layer learning application, that regime means that input features and training samples increase together while the number of hidden nodes stays fixed. Within this setting, the analysis precisely predicts parameter-estimation error and test error. The result links an inference procedure to a detailed account of its learning performance, with the fixed-width asymptotic scaling defining the scope of the prediction.
neurips-2020-matrix-inference-and-estima.tldr: ML-Mat-VAMP extends multilayer message passing to matrix-valued inference and admits exact performance predictions in a specified large-system limit.

paragraphs: Deep implicit fields represent detailed, watertight surfaces without relying on a fixed three-dimensional grid. Their flexibility is useful for shapes with different topologies, but some applications need an explicit surface mesh. The usual conversion through Marching Cubes creates an obstacle because it cannot be differentiated with respect to the underlying implicit field.

MeshSDF addresses this by examining how changes in a deep signed distance field affect nearby surface geometry. That relationship lets the authors differentiate the three-dimensional positions of surface samples with respect to the field. They use this insight to create an end-to-end differentiable mesh representation that can also change its topology.

The method connects the flexibility of implicit shape representations with applications that operate on explicit meshes. The authors validate it in single-view reconstruction using differentiable rendering and in physically driven shape optimization. In both applications, they report an advantage over state-of-the-art algorithms. These results support the value of passing optimization signals through the extracted surface, allowing the underlying shape representation to be trained for mesh-based objectives.
neurips-2020-meshsdf-differentiable-iso-.tldr: MeshSDF enables differentiable extraction of explicit meshes from deep signed distance fields, supporting topology changes and mesh-based optimization.

paragraphs: Predicting motion in a scene with multiple agents requires accounting for how those agents affect one another. A pedestrian, vehicle, or player does not move independently of surrounding entities. This paper develops a general trajectory-prediction architecture organized around inertia, relative motion, intent, and interaction, giving these motion-related patterns an explicit role in the model.

A relational component represents interactions between agents across different environments. At its center is Fuzzy Query Attention, an attention mechanism that makes continuous-valued decisions and learns corresponding responses. The use of graded decisions is motivated by the fuzzy nature of human decision making. It gives the architecture a way to model interactions without treating every decision as an all-or-nothing choice.

The authors report significant gains over existing state-of-the-art predictive models on human crowds, US freeway traffic, NBA sports data, and physics datasets. They also use ablations and augmentations to investigate how the model makes decisions and where its gains originate. The range of tested domains supports the usefulness of combining interaction modeling with motion-specific structure, beyond a single type of trajectory data.
neurips-2020-multi-agent-trajectory-pred.tldr: Fuzzy Query Attention models graded interactions between agents and improves trajectory prediction across several tested motion domains.

paragraphs: In large multilabel classification problems, an example typically receives only a few labels from a very large collection. The label vectors are therefore sparse, and the labels often have an underlying hierarchy. This paper uses both properties to reduce the computational burden of predicting labels without working directly in the full label space throughout.

The first approach constructs label groups from a low-rank nonnegative matrix factorization of the training label matrix. Classification takes place in a lower-dimensional representation, followed by a lifting step that recovers labels in the original space. This construction also supports a fast prediction algorithm with runtime logarithmic in the number of labels. A second approach partitions the label hierarchy into smaller problems that can be solved independently using the grouping method.

Experiments across many benchmark datasets show accuracy comparable to popular alternatives with significantly lower computational costs. The results make the role of label structure concrete: sparse assignments and hierarchical organization can help determine a smaller prediction problem. The contribution combines a data-dependent grouping procedure with a way to divide large label spaces into manageable parts.
neurips-2020-multilabel-classification-b.tldr: Data-dependent label grouping and hierarchical partitioning reduce multilabel classification costs while retaining comparable benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: Topological data analysis studies geometric structure in data, including how measures of shape change as a scale varies. Many applications need to vary several parameters at once, such as scale and density. Although one-parameter persistence has established statistical and machine-learning tools, the multiparameter setting lacks an equally concise representation of its results.

The paper introduces the Multiparameter Persistence Image as a descriptor suited to statistical and machine-learning frameworks. It is designed to represent information from multiparameter persistence in a usable form while remaining robust to perturbations in the data. The authors also state that it resolves finer detail than existing descriptors based on slicing and can be computed efficiently for realistically sized datasets.

They evaluate the descriptor against other multiparameter representations on several classification tasks, demonstrating its efficacy. The contribution addresses the connection between a rich mathematical description of shape and a practical input to learning algorithms. Robustness, resolution, and computational feasibility matter together here: the representation needs to preserve useful geometric information while being stable and manageable enough for downstream analysis.
neurips-2020-multiparameter-persistence-.tldr: Multiparameter Persistence Images provide a robust, efficiently computable representation of multiscale shape information for statistical and machine-learning tasks.

paragraphs: Protecting a trained model's ownership can be difficult when verification methods are vulnerable to attacks or alter the network in ways that reduce performance. This paper introduces passport-aware normalization, a formulation applicable to most existing normalization layers. It adds a private branch for ownership protection while preserving the target model's structure during ordinary inference.

The passport-aware branch is trained jointly with the model, then discarded for inference. If ownership is disputed, the private branch is attached again for verification. This arrangement separates the additional ownership-verification machinery from the deployed inference structure. The authors also combine the approach with trigger-set methods to support both black-box and white-box verification.

Experiments on image-recognition and three-dimensional point-recognition models demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The reported robustness covers fine-tuning, model compression, and ambiguity attacks, which are among the threats motivating the work. These findings support a practical protection mechanism that can be added during training and restored when verification is needed. The security claims reflect the attacks evaluated, rather than establishing resistance to every possible method of compromising ownership verification.
neurips-2020-passport-aware-normalizatio.tldr: A privately retained normalization branch enables model-ownership verification without changing the model's inference structure and withstands several tested attacks.

paragraphs: Learning a program from demonstration videos requires interpreting visual observations and finding logical behavior that explains them. Neural models can handle raw, high-dimensional inputs and noisy specifications, while rule-based synthesis explicitly captures logical rules. PLANS combines these capabilities by using a neural model to prepare the information consumed by a symbolic program synthesizer.

The neural component extracts abstract, high-level information from individual visual inputs. A rule-based system then treats that information as input-output specifications and synthesizes a program consistent with the observations. Because errors in neural perception can corrupt those specifications, the authors introduce a dynamic filtering algorithm based on selective classification to make the overall system more resistant to noisy network outputs.

PLANS achieves state-of-the-art program-synthesis performance from diverse demonstration videos in the Karel and ViZDoom environments. Training does not require ground-truth programs. The result shows the value of an intermediate specification layer: visual interpretation and logical synthesis can cooperate, provided the system also addresses uncertainty in the information passed between them. Filtering is therefore a central part of connecting learned perception to rule-based reasoning.
neurips-2020-plans-neuro-symbolic-progra.tldr: PLANS combines neural video interpretation, noise-aware specification filtering, and rule-based synthesis to learn programs without ground-truth program supervision.

paragraphs: An agent can receive many different observations even when the environment has only a small number of underlying states. This makes exploration difficult if learning depends on the size of the observation space. The paper asks when unsupervised learning can exploit that hidden structure to make reinforcement learning provably more sample-efficient.

The setting is an episodic Markov decision process whose rich observations are generated from a small latent state space. The proposed framework combines an unsupervised learning algorithm with a no-regret tabular reinforcement-learning algorithm. The guarantee is conditional: if the unsupervised component has polynomial sample complexity, the combined approach can find a near-optimal policy with sample complexity polynomial in the number of latent states.

This matters because the latent-state count can be much smaller than the number of possible observations. The guarantee connects the quality of the unsupervised learning component to efficient decision making, rather than assuming that any learned representation will suffice. The authors also instantiate the framework on a class of difficult exploration problems, providing empirical evidence that the theoretical construction can be useful in practice.
neurips-2020-provably-efficient-explorat.tldr: Under a sample-complexity guarantee for unsupervised learning, the framework learns near-optimal policies with complexity polynomial in the latent-state count.

paragraphs: This paper studies episodic reinforcement learning when transition probabilities are unknown and the objective evaluates rewards through exponential utility. A risk parameter controls whether the learner is risk-seeking or risk-averse. The authors introduce two model-free algorithms, Risk-Sensitive Value Iteration and Risk-Sensitive Q-learning, that adapt optimistic exploration to these different attitudes toward risk.

Their regret guarantees grow roughly with the square root of total interaction time, alongside factors involving states, actions, episode length, and risk sensitivity. A central feature is an exponential cost involving the magnitude of the risk parameter and the episode length. The authors also prove a lower bound: exponential dependence on these quantities is unavoidable for algorithms with square-root-time regret in the studied setting.

That lower bound supports the claimed near-optimality of the algorithms' risk-sample tradeoff, rather than treating the exponential factor as merely an implementation weakness. It persists even when the risk objective is scaled comparably to the original reward. The results distinguish sensitivity to randomness in outcomes from uncertainty caused by limited experience, and quantify how demanding stronger risk awareness can be for sample-efficient learning.
neurips-2020-risk-sensitive-reinforcemen.tldr: Two risk-sensitive learning algorithms achieve regret guarantees whose exponential risk-related cost is shown to be unavoidable for square-root-time regret.

paragraphs: Recommenders trained on implicit feedback often lack explicit negative examples. Adversarial recommendation addresses this by training a generator to supply increasingly challenging samples to a discriminator. This paper finds that sampling can be costly and that the discriminator can perform poorly in top-k recommendation. Its analysis shows that a limited-capacity generator deviates from the optimum, offering a possible explanation.

The proposed Sampling-Decomposable Generative Adversarial Recommender compensates for generator mismatch using self-normalized importance sampling. Its decomposable generator supports constant-time sample generation through the Vose-Alias method. The same structure enables alternating optimization with closed-form solutions, replacing the policy-gradient approach used by the GAN-style algorithms discussed.

Across five real-world datasets, the method outperforms IRGAN by 12.4% and the state-of-the-art recommender by 10% on average, as reported in the abstract. Discriminator training can also be 20 times faster on a dataset containing more than 120,000 items. These findings connect recommendation quality with the way training samples are produced: correcting a sampling mismatch and making generation cheaper can improve both the learned recommender and its training efficiency.
neurips-2020-sampling-decomposable-gener.tldr: SD-GAR combines importance sampling with a decomposable generator to improve recommendation performance and accelerate adversarial training.

paragraphs: Belief propagation is a fundamental method for inference in graphical models, but making it run efficiently across parallel hardware is challenging. Distributing work is only part of the problem: coordination can add overhead, and the execution strategy must also account for convergence. This paper focuses on scheduling as a way to improve practical parallel performance.

The authors adapt scalable relaxed schedulers to belief propagation. These schedulers loosen scheduling requirements to reduce the coordination overhead associated with parallel execution. The paper analytically investigates the overheads introduced by relaxation, making the scheduling tradeoff part of the algorithmic analysis rather than judging the approach solely by how much work can run simultaneously.

An extensive empirical study compares the resulting approach with previous parallel belief-propagation implementations across practical applications. The reported improvements cover both scalability and wall-clock time to convergence. Those two outcomes matter together: using more parallel hardware is useful when it also reaches the inference result sooner. The findings support relaxed scheduling as an effective implementation strategy for the applications studied, without claiming that every graphical-model inference problem benefits equally.
neurips-2020-scalable-belief-propagation.tldr: Relaxed scheduling improves the scalability and wall-clock convergence time of parallel belief propagation across the studied practical applications.

paragraphs: Cross-domain disentanglement separates a representation into information shared across domains and information specific to each domain. That separation is useful when transferring between domains or comparing their semantic content. This paper formulates the simultaneous learning of both parts using information theory, with several information constraints combined into a joint objective.

The authors derive a tractable bound on that objective and build a generative model called the Interaction Information Auto-Encoder, or IIAE. The approach does not require adversarial training or gradient reversal layers. Its formulation also provides insight into what the desired representations should preserve and how cross-domain disentanglement connects to the variational autoencoder framework.

The model is evaluated on image-to-image translation and cross-domain retrieval. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot sketch-based image retrieval without using external knowledge. These findings support the usefulness of jointly organizing shared and domain-specific information. The contribution pairs a practical generative model with an information-theoretic account of the learning objective, providing a common basis for tasks that require correspondence between different kinds of visual data.
neurips-2020-variational-interaction-inf.tldr: IIAE uses information constraints to learn shared and domain-specific representations, with strong cross-domain retrieval results without adversarial training.

paragraphs: Depth and disparity estimators often predict a distribution over a predefined set of discrete values. This creates an accuracy problem when the true value falls between those choices. The paper also identifies a training issue: learning that distribution indirectly through a regression loss causes additional difficulties in ambiguous areas, particularly near object boundaries.

The authors address both issues with a new network architecture and loss function. The architecture can output arbitrary depth values, removing the restriction to a fixed discrete set. The loss is derived from the Wasserstein distance between the predicted and true distributions, making the comparison between distributions part of the training objective itself.

Evaluations cover stereo disparity, depth estimation, and downstream three-dimensional object detection. The method substantially reduces errors in ambiguous regions, especially at object boundaries, and achieves state-of-the-art 3D object detection for autonomous driving. The downstream result matters because boundary errors affect where objects are located in three-dimensional space. Improving how depth is represented and trained can therefore benefit a later perception task as well as the depth estimate itself.
neurips-2020-wasserstein-distances-for-s.tldr: Arbitrary-valued depth predictions and a Wasserstein-based loss reduce boundary errors and improve downstream 3D object detection.

paragraphs: Regret bounds describe how much reward a learning agent loses relative to optimal behavior as it gains experience. This paper improves bounds that depend on the difficulty of a particular finite episodic Markov decision process. It does so by changing how the relevant gaps between decisions are defined, rather than relying only on earlier value-function gap definitions.

The key observation is that favorable regret does not require learning optimal behavior in states that an optimal policy never reaches. The alternative gaps account for this distinction. Using them, the authors prove tighter upper bounds for optimistic algorithms and derive new information-theoretic lower bounds for a large class of Markov decision processes.

The comparison also exposes a limitation of optimistic algorithms: they cannot achieve the information-theoretic lower bounds even in deterministic environments unless the optimal policy is unique. Uniqueness is stated as a necessary condition here, not a sufficient guarantee of attaining the bound. The work therefore refines both the description of instance difficulty and the understanding of when optimism falls short of the best theoretically possible regret.
neurips-2021-beyond-value-function-gaps-.tldr: Reachability-aware gap definitions tighten reinforcement-learning regret bounds and reveal limits of optimism when optimal policies are not unique.

paragraphs: The forward-backward representation aims to learn environment dynamics before a task's reward is specified. During an unsupervised phase, reward-free interactions train two representations using deep learning and temporal-difference learning. This phase assumes access to an exploration scheme or replay buffer. The learned representation captures long-range state-action relationships through a predictive occupancy map.

When a reward becomes available, the method estimates its representation from reward observations or an explicit description, such as a target state. It then obtains a policy directly from the representations, without planning. The guarantee depends on training quality: perfect training yields provably optimal policies for any reward function, while imperfect training produces suboptimality proportional to the unsupervised approximation error.

The approach compares well with goal-oriented reinforcement-learning algorithms on discrete and continuous mazes, pixel-based MsPacman, and the FetchReach virtual robot arm. The authors also demonstrate immediate adaptation to new tasks beyond goal-oriented learning. The central contribution is reusable control knowledge: the initial representation can support rewards introduced afterward without synthesizing states as in model-based approaches or requiring a planning stage for each new task.
neurips-2021-learning-one-representation.tldr: Forward-backward representations turn reward-free experience into policies for later-specified rewards, with optimality guarantees tied to representation accuracy.
